hints: Focus on what each definition equation actually produces on the right hand side, ions or just neutral atoms.
Recall the first ionisation equation, $\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^+(\text{g}) + e^-$, which clearly makes a $1+$ ion.
Compare heterolytic fission which splits both electrons to one atom, with atomisation which only makes gaseous atoms from an element.
walkthrough:
**Recall first ionisation energy**

Think of removing one electron from a neutral gaseous atom. That must leave a positive ion behind.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^+(\text{g}) + e^-$$

**Recall heterolytic fission**

Think of a covalent bond breaking unevenly. Both shared electrons go to one atom, so one fragment becomes positive and the other negative.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{H-Cl(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}^+(\text{g}) + \text{Cl}^-(\text{g})$$

**Recall enthalpy change of atomisation**

Think of making separate gaseous atoms from an element. No electrons are lost or gained, so no ions are formed.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Na(s)} \rightarrow \text{Na(g)}$$

**Combine the conclusions**

Statements 1 and 2 both include formation of a positive ion, but statement 3 gives only neutral atoms. So only 1 and 2 are correct.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes all three statements. Statement 3 is atomisation to neutral gaseous atoms, for example $\text{Mg(s)} \rightarrow \text{Mg(g)}$, with no positive ion formed.
options.B: Correct because only 1 and 2 involve a positive ion. First ionisation gives $\text{X}^+(\text{g}) + e^-$ and heterolytic fission gives a cation plus an anion, for example $\text{H}^+ + \text{Cl}^-$.
options.C: Incorrect because it pairs 2 and 3. While 2 is correct, 3 is wrong since atomisation produces neutral atoms, not ions.
options.D: Incorrect because it includes only 1. Statement 1 is correct, but statement 2 is also correct since heterolytic fission can form a positive ion such as $\text{CH}_3^+$ from $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$.
